questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-1)^{2}=-5(x-1)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(1,1).$ So we have

$$
x-1=p{t}^{2},\,y-1=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p(x-1) & =-5(x-1) \\ 4p & =-5 \\ p & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-1=(-\frac{5}{4}){t}^{2},\,y-1=2(-\frac{5}{4})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-1=-\frac{5}{4}{t}^{2},\,y-1=-\frac{5}{2}t.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-2=3t,\,y+2=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =\frac{x-2}{3},\,{t}^{2}=\frac{2(y+2)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(\frac{x-2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{2(y+2)}{3}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & =\frac{2(y+2)}{3} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =9\cdot (\frac{2(y+2)}{3}) \\ (x-2)^{2} & =6(y+2).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation $(y-5)^{2}=2(x-2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h)$ that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case $(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),$ we see that the parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(2,5).$ So we have

$$
x-2=p{t}^{2},\,y-5=2pt.
$$

Now, comparing the right-hand sides of the given Cartesian equation and the general case, then solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4p(x-h) & =2(x-2) \\ 4p(x-2) & =2(x-2) \\ 4p & =2 \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x-2=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},\,y-5=2(\frac{1}{2})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x-2=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2},\,y-5=t.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x-2=-4t,\,y-5=-2{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =-\frac{x-2}{4},\,{t}^{2}=-\frac{y-5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{x-2}{4})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-\frac{y-5}{2}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16} & =-\frac{y-5}{2} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-8(y-5).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following parametric equation of the parabola

$$
x+7=-3t,\,y-2=-9{t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this parabola is

$(x\,+$

questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}t & =-\frac{x+7}{3},\,{t}^{2}=-\frac{1}{9}(y-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={(-\frac{x+7}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(x+7)^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-\frac{1}{9}(y-2)$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+7)^{2}}{9} & =-\frac{1}{9}(y-2) \\ {(x+7)}^{2} & =-(y-2)\end{aligned}
$$
